questions.statement: What are the main parts of a typical English story?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A setting, characters, events and an ending
options.feedback: These four elements together give a story its structure from beginning to end.

options.text: A title, a margin and a page number
options.feedback: Those are features of a printed page, not the parts of a narrative.

options.text: A topic sentence in each of five paragraphs
options.feedback: That structure belongs to an essay, not to a story with characters and events.

options.text: A list of facts presented alphabetically
options.feedback: Alphabetical lists belong to reference material, not to a narrative.

questions.explanation: A story usually moves through a setting, a series of events, characters and a conclusion that resolves the central problem.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best opening line for a story about a boy who finds a bicycle in the river.
questions.context: A creative writing exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: This story is about a boy named Tomas and about a bicycle and about a river.
options.feedback: The opening lists the elements of the story instead of beginning it.

options.text: The bicycle surfaced from the river exactly as Tomas reached the bank.
options.feedback: The line introduces the character and the key event in the same moment, which pulls the reader in.

options.text: Rivers have many uses, and a history of rivers is very long.
options.feedback: The general comment about rivers does not begin the story at all.

options.text: In this paragraph I am going to explain the meaning of the word bicycle.
options.feedback: That is the language of an essay, not the language of a narrative.

questions.explanation: A strong opening enters the action quickly and gives the reader a reason to keep reading, rather than starting with long background.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the setting of a story tell the reader?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The order in which the events take place
options.feedback: That is the order of events, which is a separate element of the story.

options.text: The lesson the reader should learn
options.feedback: Any lesson is drawn by the reader; the setting itself states only place and time.

options.text: The time and place where the events occur
options.feedback: The setting establishes where and when the narrative takes place.

options.text: The reason the story was written
options.feedback: The purpose of the author is not part of the setting.

questions.explanation: The setting gives the time and the place where the story happens, and it shapes how the events can occur.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best way to build tension in a short story.
questions.context: A creative writing task in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Describing the colour of the walls at length
options.feedback: Long description of scenery slows the action down without creating any stakes.

options.text: Repeating the same sentence five times for effect
options.feedback: Repetition without rising stakes adds no pressure to the outcome.

options.text: Ending the story as soon as the problem appears
options.feedback: Resolving at once removes the uncertainty that produces tension.

options.text: Introducing a problem that matters to the character and delaying its solution
options.feedback: Stakes combined with delay create suspense, which is the engine of narrative tension.

questions.explanation: Tension grows when a problem appears and something is at stake for the character, so raising the difficulty of a problem is the standard technique.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best ending for a story about a student who wanted to join the school band.
questions.context: A creative writing exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: She auditioned for the band that year and nothing more was ever written about it.
options.feedback: The story stops without resolving the question it created for the reader.

options.text: Bands are popular in many schools and students often audition for them.
options.feedback: A general comment replaces the resolution and abandons the character entirely.

options.text: She never wanted to join the band and she never considered doing so.
options.feedback: The ending contradicts the whole premise the story was built on.

options.text: She auditioned with no confidence, was unsure at first, and was then invited to join the band for the term.
options.feedback: The ending answers the question about whether she would be accepted, with the uncertainty that makes it believable.

questions.explanation: A satisfying ending resolves the question the story raised, whether that resolution is fully successful or only partly so.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best shows a character's action rather than telling a feeling?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: He was very nervous about the interview, which he felt strongly.
options.feedback: The sentence names the feeling directly and adds no observable behaviour.

options.text: He thought about the interview and it made him anxious.
options.feedback: The sentence reports the internal state instead of showing anything the reader can see.

options.text: He checked the door twice, wiped his palms and said nothing at all.
options.feedback: The actions let the reader infer the nervousness without being told about it.

options.text: His nervousness was present and clearly noticeable.
options.feedback: The sentence repeats the label without any concrete action attached to it.

questions.explanation: Showing means letting the reader see the behaviour directly, while telling names the feeling without demonstrating it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the role of the problem in a story?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: It appears only in the final sentence of the story
options.feedback: A problem stated at the end cannot drive anything, because the story has finished.

options.text: It creates the obstacle that drives the events forward
options.feedback: Without a problem there is no reason for the events to unfold as they do.

options.text: It is decoration added to make the text longer
options.feedback: The problem gives the story its purpose rather than padding its length.

options.text: It replaces the characters entirely in the middle section
options.feedback: The characters continue to act in the presence of the problem rather than being replaced.

questions.explanation: The problem is the obstacle that drives the events and gives the narrative its purpose and direction.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct sequence for the parts of a story.
questions.context: A planning exercise in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Setting, problem, events, conflict, resolution
options.feedback: This order introduces where things happen, what goes wrong, and how it ends.

options.text: Resolution, setting, problem, events, conflict
options.feedback: The story would begin with how it ends, which destroys the sequence of cause and effect.

options.text: Conflict, resolution, setting, problem, events
options.feedback: Starting with conflict before the setting leaves the reader with no context.

options.text: Events, setting, problem, resolution, conflict
options.feedback: Events cannot come before the setting that makes them possible.

questions.explanation: A narrative moves from the setting to the introduction of the problem, through the events and the conflict, and ends with a resolution.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb in a story sentence shows action most strongly?
questions.context: A creative writing lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: He did something with the younger child during the emergency.
options.feedback: The phrase reports an event without any picture of what actually happened.

options.text: He sprinted across the yard and pulled the younger child clear.
options.feedback: Sprinted and pulled give movement and force, which make the moment visible.

options.text: He was involved in the situation that occurred at that time.
options.feedback: The phrasing reports involvement without showing any concrete action.

options.text: He made a movement related to the child who was there.
options.feedback: The phrase is vague and gives the reader no image of the event.

questions.explanation: A precise verb of movement or change creates a vivid image, while a general verb such as did leaves the reader with no picture.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word 'flashback' mean in a story?
questions.context: A reading and writing lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A summary of the whole story given at the start
options.feedback: That is a prologue or an abstract, which is not a flashback.

options.text: A quick repetition of a sentence for emphasis
options.feedback: Repetition for effect is a rhetorical device, not a shift in narrative time.

options.text: A disagreement between two characters in the story
options.feedback: A dispute between characters is a conflict, which is a separate narrative element.

options.text: A scene set earlier that explains the present events
options.feedback: A flashback moves back in time and usually clarifies why the present action happens.

questions.explanation: A flashback interrupts the present action of a narrative to show an earlier event that explains the characters or the situation.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best sentence for the ending of a story about a lost dog that finally finds its owner.
questions.context: A creative writing exercise in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Dogs sometimes wander and sometimes they come back, which is a fact of nature.
options.feedback: The general observation replaces the resolution with a comment about dogs.

options.text: The dog was lost and the owner was worried and the search went on all day.
options.feedback: The sentence restates the situation instead of ending it.

options.text: The dog pushed its way through the crowd and stopped, wagging, in front of the woman who had been searching since dawn.
options.feedback: The ending brings the search to a close with an image that confirms the reunion.

options.text: Nobody in this story ever found the dog again at any point.
options.feedback: The sentence contradicts the premise the story has been building towards.

questions.explanation: A good ending resolves the central question of the story and leaves the reader with a settled feeling about what happened.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why do writers use dialogue in a story?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To reveal the thoughts of characters and move the story forward
options.feedback: Speech shows what characters feel and often advances the action at the same time.

options.text: To fill space on the page with words
options.feedback: Dialogue is used for effect, not to lengthen a text arbitrarily.

options.text: To replace the need for a clear setting
options.feedback: A story still needs a setting; dialogue does not replace that element.

options.text: To guarantee that every reader enjoys the plot
options.feedback: No technique can ensure that, and dialogue is not used for that purpose.

questions.explanation: Dialogue lets characters reveal their thoughts and relationships directly and makes a narrative move faster than narration alone.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that best shows rising tension near the end of a story.
questions.context: A writing assessment in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: He reached the bank, sat down and then had something to eat.
options.feedback: The problem is over by this point, so the tension has already been released.

options.text: The river was long and the day was sunny and the walk was pleasant.
options.feedback: The description is calm and unthreatening, which works against any sense of danger.

options.text: He had crossed the river many times and knew the route well.
options.feedback: Familiarity removes the uncertainty that a tense moment depends on.

options.text: The rope slipped another inch and the water was already at his knees.
options.feedback: The growing danger and the pressure of the moment make the outcome uncertain.

questions.explanation: Tension rises when the danger increases and the outcome becomes less certain, which these sentences express through urgency and unresolved pressure.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the story sentence: 'The door would not open, and from inside came a sound that nobody in the house could explain.'
questions.context: A creative writing task in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The sound was a clear and pleasant ring of the doorbell pressed once.
options.feedback: A friendly bell sound resolves the mystery instead of creating one.

options.text: The sound was slow and uneven and nothing in the house explained it.
options.feedback: The unexplained sound raises a question the next part of the story will have to answer.

options.text: The sound was a friendly voice saying that everything was fine.
options.feedback: The reassurance ends the tension rather than sustaining it.

options.text: The sound was an explanation of exactly what had happened earlier.
options.feedback: Giving the explanation here removes the uncertainty the sentence needs to create.

questions.explanation: To create suspense the sentence should introduce an unexpected sound or presence without explaining it, leaving the reader wanting to know more.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a writer check when reviewing a story for coherence?
questions.context: A writing skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: That the events follow from one another and the problem is resolved
options.feedback: Logical sequence and a solved central problem are what make a narrative coherent.

options.text: That every sentence is exactly the same length as the one before it
options.feedback: Uniform sentence length has no bearing on whether the events hang together.

options.text: That no word appears more than once in the whole text
options.feedback: Repeating words is normal and does not damage the coherence of a story.

options.text: That the text contains no more than two paragraphs
options.feedback: The number of paragraphs is a matter of length and pacing, not of coherence.

questions.explanation: A coherent story has events that follow one another logically and a resolution that answers the problem the narrative raised.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best description of a main character in a story.
questions.context: A creative writing exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A character defined only by height, eye colour and age
options.feedback: Physical details alone do not explain why a character matters to the plot.

options.text: A character who appears in the first paragraph and then disappears
options.feedback: Appearing briefly does not make a character main; involvement in the conflict does.

options.text: A character defined by what they want and by the choices they make
options.feedback: Desire and choice are what make a character central to the plot.

options.text: A character whose name is repeated most often in the text
options.feedback: Repetition of a name is a technical detail, not what makes a character central.

questions.explanation: A main character is defined by what the character wants and by how they respond to the central problem, not by a list of physical details.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the function of the narrator in a story?
questions.context: A reading comprehension lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To write the dialogue for every character in the story
options.feedback: Characters speak for themselves; the narrator reports and frames their actions.

options.text: To tell the events and decide what the reader knows
options.feedback: The narrator presents the action and controls the information given to the reader.

options.text: To prove that the events really happened as described
options.feedback: A narrator is part of the fiction and does not certify real events.

options.text: To decide how long the story should be before it is written
options.feedback: Length is a structural choice of the writer, not the defining role of the narrator.

questions.explanation: The narrator is the voice that tells the story and decides what the reader is allowed to know about the events.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word 'plot' mean in a story?
questions.context: A creative writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The sequence of events in the story
options.feedback: The plot is the chain of events that carries the narrative forward.

options.text: The list of characters who appear in the story
options.feedback: That list is the cast of the story, not the plot.

options.text: The physical appearance of the main character
options.feedback: Description of appearance is a matter of detail rather than of plot.

options.text: The number of pages in the story
options.feedback: Length is a property of the text and not what the word 'plot' denotes.

questions.explanation: The plot is the sequence of events that makes up the narrative, arranged so that one event leads to the next.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why should a writer open a story with action rather than with long description?
questions.context: A creative writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Because description is never used in modern stories
options.feedback: Description does appear in stories, though usually after the action has begun.

options.text: Because action is always easier to write than description
options.feedback: The claim is not true; precise description is among the hardest things to write.

options.text: It draws the reader into the events before attention fades
options.feedback: The immediate action creates a question the reader wants answered.

options.text: Because readers never notice descriptive sentences
options.feedback: Readers notice them, and a long opening description often loses their interest.

questions.explanation: An action opening puts the reader inside the story immediately, which creates curiosity about what will happen next.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should happen to a problem that a story never resolves?
questions.context: A creative writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The reader is left wanting a longer version of the same story
options.feedback: Suspense about the outcome is different from a problem that simply never closes.

options.text: The reader is left wanting to read a different author's work
options.feedback: That reaction follows from tedium rather than from an unresolved problem.

options.text: The reader is left wanting to rewrite the story themselves
options.feedback: That reaction follows from poor quality writing, not from an open ending.

options.text: The reader is left unsure how the story ends
options.feedback: An unresolved central problem denies the reader the satisfaction the plot promised.

questions.explanation: A narrative that leaves its central problem unresolved frustrates the reader, so the ending must address what became of it.
questions.subject: ingles
